dryRun.title: Insert 5 into the search tree 8 (3 (1, 6), 10)
rows: put 5 here as the left child of 6
dryRun.note: In a BST everything to the left is smaller and everything to the right is bigger. So each comparison throws away one whole side, like binary search. Search, insert and delete all follow one path from the root.

think.q:
function insert(n, v) {
  if (!n) return { val: v, left: null, right: null }
  if (v < n.val) n.left = insert(n.left, v)
  else n.right = insert(n.right, v)
  return n
}
let root = null
for (const v of [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]) root = insert(root, v)
const out = []
const walk = (n) => { if (!n) return; walk(n.left); out.push(n.val); walk(n.right) }
walk(root)
console.log(out.join(","))
why: Whatever order values go in, a BST keeps them arranged so an inorder walk gives sorted values: 1, 3, 4, 5, 8.
The shape depends on the insert order, but the inorder result does not.

think.q:
function insert(n, v) {
  if (!n) return { val: v, left: null, right: null }
  if (v < n.val) n.left = insert(n.left, v)
  else n.right = insert(n.right, v)
  return n
}
const height = (n) => (n ? 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right)) : 0)
let root = null
for (const v of [1, 2, 3, 4]) root = insert(root, v)
console.log(height(root))
why: Sorted input makes every new value the right child of the last one: a straight line with height 4.
Then search costs O(n), not O(log n). This is why balanced trees exist.

think.q: A tree is 5 (1, 6 (3, 7)). Every node is bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child. Is it a valid BST?
opts: Yes, every parent-child pair is fine
No, 3 is in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5
why: The rule is for the whole subtree, not just the direct child. Everything under the right child of 5 must be greater than 5, and 3 is not.
So when validating, pass down a min and a max that every node must stay inside.

think.q: What is the cost of search in a BST with n nodes and height h?
opts: O(h), which is O(log n) if balanced and O(n) if it is a line
why: One path from the root, so the cost is the height. Balanced trees keep h near log n.
A plain BST gives no guarantee, so say "O(h)" in an interview.

think.q: You delete a node that has two children. What is the usual way to do it?
opts: Copy in the smallest value of the right subtree (the inorder successor), then delete that node
Move the left child up and drop the right child
Mark it as empty and leave it
why: The inorder successor is the next bigger value, so putting it in the node's place keeps the BST rule true.
Nodes with zero or one child are easy: remove them, and connect the parent to the single child.

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }. Write isValidBST(root). Return true if the tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger (no duplicates allowed). An empty tree is valid.
try.hint: Write a helper check(node, min, max) that needs min < node.val < max. Going left, the new max is node.val. Going right, the new min is node.val. Start with -Infinity and Infinity.

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isValidBST(T(2, T(1), T(3))) === true, "expected true")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isValidBST(T(5, T(1), T(4, T(3), T(6)))) === false, "expected false")

checks.t: the deep violation (3 under the right side of 5)
checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isValidBST(T(5, T(1), T(6, T(3), T(7)))) === false, "expected false, check the whole subtree")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isValidBST(T(2, T(2), T(3))) === false && isValidBST(T(2, T(1), T(2))) === false, "expected false for equal values")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isValidBST(null) === true && isValidBST(T(1)) === true, "expected true")

takeaway.key: A BST keeps smaller on the left, larger on the right for the whole subtree. Search, insert and delete cost O(h): O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if it is a line. Inorder gives sorted values.
mistakes: Validating only parent versus child, not the whole subtree (use min and max).
Using < where equal values must be rejected.
Inserting sorted data and getting a straight line.
Forgetting to return the node from a recursive insert, so the link is lost.

dryRun.title: Diameter of the tree 1 (2 (4, 5), 3), in edges. Height is counted in nodes (empty = 0)
dryRun.note: The longest path through a node is left height + right height. Postorder gives each node its children's heights, so one pass is enough: O(n).

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
const height = (n) => (n ? 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right)) : 0)
console.log(height(root), height(root.right), height(null))
why: The longest path from the root is 1, 2, 4: three nodes. The node 3 alone is height 1. An empty tree is 0 here.
Some books count edges and make an empty tree -1. Always check which one the question uses.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
let best = 0
function h(n) {
  if (!n) return 0
  const l = h(n.left), r = h(n.right)
  best = Math.max(best, l + r)
  return 1 + Math.max(l, r)
}
h(root)
console.log(best)
why: At the root, l = 2 and r = 1, so the path 4-2-1-3 has 3 edges.
Note the function returns the height but records the diameter in a side variable. Those are two different numbers.

think.q: Is the diameter (the longest path between any two nodes) always the path that goes through the root?
opts: No, a deep subtree can hold a longer path that never touches the root
why: If the left subtree is a long zig-zag and the right side is tiny, the longest path stays inside the left subtree.
That is why we check l + r at every node and keep the maximum.

think.q: Which statement is correct?
opts: Depth of a node counts down from the node to its deepest leaf
Height of a node counts up from the node to the root
Depth of a node counts from the root to that node; height counts from the node down to its deepest leaf
Depth and height are the same
why: Depth looks up (how far from the root). Height looks down (how far to the farthest leaf below).
The root has depth 0, and the height of the tree is the root's height.

think.q: A solution calls height() on both children at every node to get the diameter. What is its worst-case time?
why: In a line-shaped tree, each height call walks almost the whole tree, and it is called at every node. That is O(n²).
Computing the heights and the best path in the same recursion fixes it: O(n).

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }. Write diameter(root). Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. An empty tree or a single node gives 0. It must be O(n).
try.hint: Write a helper h(node) that returns the height (empty = 0). Inside it, after getting l and r, update best = Math.max(best, l + r).

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(diameter(T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))) === 3, "expected 3")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(diameter(null) === 0 && diameter(T(1)) === 0, "expected 0")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(diameter(T(1, T(2, T(3, T(4)), null), null)) === 3, "expected 3")

checks.t: the longest path does not touch the root
checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); const left = T(2, T(3, T(5), T(6)), T(4, T(7), T(8))); assert(diameter(T(1, left, null)) === 4, "expected 4")
let t = null; for (let i = 0; i < 5000; i++) t = { val: i, left: t, right: null }; const t0 = Date.now(); assert(diameter(t) === 4999 && Date.now() - t0 < 200, "wrong or too slow, it must be O(n)")

takeaway.key: Height looks down, depth looks up. Compute heights in postorder and use the same pass to record the best left + right at every node: diameter in O(n).
mistakes: Assuming the diameter goes through the root.
Calling a separate height() at every node and getting O(n²).
Mixing edges and nodes when counting.
Returning the diameter from the helper instead of the height.

dryRun.title: Build a tree from preorder [3, 9, 20, 15, 7] and inorder [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]
dryRun.note: The first item of preorder is the root. Find it in inorder: everything on its left is the left subtree, everything on its right is the right subtree. Repeat on each piece.

think.q:
const pre = [3, 9, 20, 15, 7], ino = [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]
const idx = new Map(ino.map((v, i) => [v, i]))
let p = 0
function build(lo, hi) {
  if (lo > hi) return null
  const v = pre[p++]
  const m = idx.get(v)
  const node = { val: v, left: null, right: null }
  node.left = build(lo, m - 1)
  node.right = build(m + 1, hi)
  return node
}
const root = build(0, ino.length - 1)
console.log(root.val, root.left.val, root.right.val, root.right.left.val)
why: 3 is the root. 9 is the only value left of 3 in inorder, so it is the left child. The right part 15 20 7 has 20 as its root (next in preorder), and 15 is to its left.
The pointer p walks through preorder once. The order of the two recursive calls matters: left first, because preorder lists the left subtree before the right.

think.q: Why is the preorder list alone not enough to rebuild the tree?
opts: It names the root but does not say where the left subtree ends and the right begins
why: Preorder gives root, then all of the left subtree, then all of the right subtree, but nothing marks the border between them.
Inorder shows the border: the position of the root splits the left values from the right values.

think.q: The code stores each inorder value's index in a Map. What does that improve?
opts: Finding the root in inorder becomes O(1), so the whole build is O(n) instead of O(n²)
why: Without the map, each node would scan inorder to find its root: O(n) per node. With it, one lookup.
This needs all values to be unique, which interview versions promise.

think.q: Which pair of traversals is not enough to rebuild one unique binary tree?
why: Preorder and postorder both give the root but never separate left from right. A node with a single child could be either a left or a right child.
Any pair that includes inorder works, because inorder always shows the split.

think.q: You build from postorder and inorder. Where is the root, and which subtree do you build first?
opts: The first item; the left subtree first
The last item; the right subtree first
The last item; the left subtree first
why: Postorder is left, right, root, so reading it from the end gives root, then right, then left. That is why the right subtree is built first.
Mixing this order up is the classic bug.

try.task: Write buildTree(preorder, inorder). Both arrays hold the same unique values. Return the root of the tree as nodes { val, left, right } (missing children are null). Return null for empty input.
try.hint: Map each inorder value to its index. Keep a pointer p into preorder. build(lo, hi) takes pre[p++] as the root, finds m, then builds left from lo..m-1 and right from m+1..hi.

checks.verify: const ser = (n) => (n ? [n.val, ser(n.left), ser(n.right)] : null); assert(JSON.stringify(ser(buildTree([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]))) === '[3,[9,null,null],[20,[15,null,null],[7,null,null]]]', "wrong tree")
const ser = (n) => (n ? [n.val, ser(n.left), ser(n.right)] : null); assert(JSON.stringify(ser(buildTree([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1]))) === '[1,[2,[3,null,null],null],null]', "wrong tree")
const ser = (n) => (n ? [n.val, ser(n.left), ser(n.right)] : null); assert(JSON.stringify(ser(buildTree([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]))) === '[1,null,[2,null,[3,null,null]]]', "wrong tree")

checks.t: empty input and a single node
checks.verify: assert(buildTree([], []) === null, "expected null"); const r = buildTree([5], [5]); assert(r && r.val === 5 && r.left === null && r.right === null, "single node")

const n = 5000; const pre = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i); const ino = [...pre].reverse(); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = buildTree(pre, ino); assert(r && r.val === 0 && Date.now() - t0 < 300, "wrong or too slow, did you search inorder every time?")

takeaway.key: In preorder the first item is the root. Its position in inorder splits left from right. Use a Map for O(1) lookups and build left before right: O(n).
mistakes: Building the right subtree before the left when reading preorder.
Scanning inorder for every root (O(n²)).
Slicing arrays at every step, which copies a lot of data.
Trying preorder + postorder only (not unique).

dryRun.title: Iterative inorder of the tree 1 (2 (4, 5), 3)
rows: go left as far as possible, push 1, 2, 4
pop 2, visit, then go right to 5 and push it
pop 1, visit, then go right to 3 and push it
dryRun.note: The stack plays the part of the recursion's call stack. After you pop and visit a node, you step into its right child and again go as far left as possible.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
const out = []
const stack = [root]
while (stack.length) {
  const n = stack.pop()
  out.push(n.val)
  if (n.right) stack.push(n.right)
  if (n.left) stack.push(n.left)
}
console.log(out.join(","))
why: This is an iterative preorder. Pop the node, visit it, then push its children.
Push the right child first, so the left child is on top and comes out first.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
const out = []
const st = [root]
while (st.length) {
  const n = st.pop()
  out.push(n.val)
  if (n.left) st.push(n.left)
  if (n.right) st.push(n.right)
}
console.log(out.reverse().join(","))
why: This loop visits node, right, left, which gives 1,3,2,5,4. Reversing that gives left, right, node: the postorder 4,5,2,3,1.
A neat trick: postorder is the reverse of "node, right, left".

think.q:
let root = null
for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) root = { val: i, left: root, right: null }
const depth = (n) => (n ? 1 + depth(n.left) : 0)
try {
  console.log(depth(root))
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.constructor.name)
}
why: The tree is a line 100,000 nodes deep. The recursion needs 100,000 stack frames, and JavaScript allows only about ten thousand. It throws a RangeError.
An explicit stack lives on the heap, so it can be as deep as memory allows.

think.q: In an iterative preorder, you pop a node and push both children. Which child do you push first?
why: A stack gives back the last item pushed first. To visit the left subtree before the right, the left child must be pushed last.
With a queue the rule flips, and you get BFS.

think.q: Compared with recursive DFS, what does the iterative version change?
opts: Nothing in big-O (still O(n) time, O(h) space), but it avoids stack overflow
It visits nodes in a different order
why: The same nodes are visited the same number of times, and the stack still holds a path of up to h nodes.
The gain is safety on very deep trees and more control over the traversal.

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }. Write inorderIter(root). Return the inorder values without recursion. It must work on a tree that is 100,000 nodes deep.
try.hint: Keep cur = root and a stack. While cur or the stack is not empty: push and go left while you can; then pop, visit, and set cur to the popped node's right child.

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorderIter(T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3)))) === "[4,2,5,1,3]", "expected [4,2,5,1,3]")

checks.t: a search tree gives sorted values
checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorderIter(T(4, T(2, T(1), T(3)), T(6, T(5), T(7))))) === "[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]", "expected 1 to 7")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorderIter(null)) === "[]" && JSON.stringify(inorderIter(T(8))) === "[8]", "edge cases")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorderIter(T(1, null, T(2, null, T(3))))) === "[1,2,3]", "expected [1,2,3]")

let t = null; for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) t = { val: i, left: t, right: null }; const r = inorderIter(t); assert(r.length === 100000 && r[0] === 0 && r[99999] === 99999, "wrong result for the deep tree")

takeaway.key: Replace the call stack with your own stack. Inorder: go left pushing, pop and visit, then step right. Same O(n) time, but it survives very deep trees.
mistakes: Pushing the left child before the right in preorder (the order flips).
Forgetting to move to cur.right after visiting.
Stopping when cur is null even though the stack is not empty.
Using a queue and getting BFS by accident.

dryRun.title: Insert 1, 2, 3 into an AVL tree
rows: rotate left at 1: now 2 is the root with children 1 and 3
dryRun.note: AVL rule: at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. A rotation fixes a broken node in O(1) and keeps the inorder order.

think.q:
const n3 = { val: 3, left: null, right: null }
const n2 = { val: 2, left: null, right: n3 }
const n1 = { val: 1, left: null, right: n2 }
function rotateLeft(x) {
  const y = x.right
  x.right = y.left
  y.left = x
  return y
}
const r = rotateLeft(n1)
console.log(r.val, r.left.val, r.right.val)
why: The line 1 → 2 → 3 becomes a tree with 2 on top, 1 on the left and 3 on the right. The height drops from 3 to 2.
The inorder order is still 1, 2, 3, so the search-tree rule still holds.

think.q: Which condition must hold at every node of an AVL tree?
opts: Both subtrees have the same number of nodes
The heights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1
All leaves are at the same depth
why: It is about heights, not about node counts. This loose rule is enough to keep the height at about 1.44 × log₂(n).
Red-black trees use a different, looser colour rule with the same O(log n) result.

think.q: What do balanced BSTs guarantee for search, insert and delete?
why: Because the height is always O(log n), and every operation follows one path plus a few rotations.
A plain BST has only an average guarantee on random data.

think.q: Do you usually need to write an AVL or red-black tree from scratch in a coding interview?
opts: Yes, it is a very common question
Rarely. Know why they exist, what a rotation does, and the O(log n) guarantee
Never, and you should not mention them
why: Most interviews ask for a plain BST, or for using a sorted structure. You are expected to explain the idea, not to code the rebalancing.
JavaScript has no built-in balanced tree, so you would also name the trade-off of writing one yourself.

think.q: Which of these is typically built on a balanced search tree?
opts: An ordered map or set (for example Java's TreeMap or C++ std::map)
why: Ordered maps keep keys sorted, so they support "next bigger key" and range queries in O(log n). A hash map cannot do that.
Databases use a related structure, the B-tree, for their indexes.

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }. Write isBalanced(root). Return true if, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. An empty tree is balanced. It must be O(n).
try.hint: Write h(node) that returns the height, or -1 as a signal when the subtree is already unbalanced. Check the two child heights and return early if either is -1 or they differ by more than 1.

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isBalanced(T(3, T(9), T(20, T(15), T(7)))) === true, "expected true")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isBalanced(T(1, null, T(2, null, T(3)))) === false, "expected false")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isBalanced(null) === true && isBalanced(T(1)) === true, "expected true")

checks.t: balanced at the root but not deeper
checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(isBalanced(T(1, T(2, T(3, T(4), null), null), T(5))) === false, "expected false, the node 2 is unbalanced")

let t = null; for (let i = 0; i < 5000; i++) t = { val: i, left: t, right: null }; const t0 = Date.now(); assert(isBalanced(t) === false && Date.now() - t0 < 200, "wrong or too slow, it must be O(n)")

takeaway.key: A balanced BST keeps its height near log n, so search, insert and delete are O(log n) worst case. Rotations repair an imbalance in O(1) and keep the sorted order.
mistakes: Checking balance only at the root, not at every node.
Computing heights again at every node (O(n²)).
Thinking balanced means perfectly full.
Expecting to hand-code AVL in a normal interview instead of explaining it.

flags: construct-tree: the try-it expected trees were produced by a reference build in the generator and written into the checks. Example 1 matches the classic answer 3 (9, 20 (15, 7)).
tree-measurements: the "does not touch the root" check expects 4 (path 5-3-2-4-7, while the longest path through the root is only 3).
dfs-iterative: the 100,000 node check relies on the Node/browser stack limit being below 100,000 frames, which holds today.
balanced-bst: the try-it asks for isBalanced, not a real AVL insert, because a rotation-based AVL is too long for a self-check. The lesson text and rotation question cover the idea.
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (concept dry runs are not machine-run).
